“A century before decision theory existed” is questionable: Pascal's wager dates from the 1650s-1660s; expected-utility reasoning is usually dated to Bernoulli (1738) and formal decision theory to the 20th century. Translated as written.

accroche: It is not an argument for believing. It is an argument for those for whom proofs are not enough.
contenu_vulgarise:
The fragment is famous and rarely read. In the *Pensées* (*Thoughts*), under the title “Infinite, Nothing,” Pascal develops a line of reasoning usually summed up this way: wager that God exists, you have nothing to lose and everything to gain.

Summed up like that, the wager seems cynical, almost commercial. The text does something else.

## Whom It Addresses

Pascal does not claim to prove the existence of God. He writes it explicitly: reason cannot decide. God is, or he is not, but to which side shall we incline? Reason can determine nothing here.

The argument is therefore tailored to a precise situation: that of someone whom proofs have not convinced, and who cannot settle into indifference either, because he is staking his life anyway. This is the point most often glossed over: according to Pascal, one cannot *not* wager. To live is already to have placed a stake.

## The Structure

Next comes the calculation. If you bet on the existence of God and you are right, the gain is infinite. If you are wrong, the loss is finite, a few pleasures. A chance of infinite gain against a bounded loss: whatever the probability, even a very small one, the calculation tips the same way.

This is, formally, an expected-value argument applied to a decision, a century before decision theory existed. Pascal, who had just founded the calculus of probabilities in his correspondence with Fermat, applies his own tool here to an unexpected object.

## The Objections, Some of Which He Knew

The strongest is an old one: why that god? The reasoning works for any divinity promising an infinite gain, and these divinities exclude one another. The wager, if it holds, proves too much.

Another concerns sincerity: one does not decide to believe as one decides to bet. Pascal anticipated it, and his answer is disconcerting: he advises acting first, following the gestures and habits, admitting that conviction may follow. Belief, for him, has less to do with intellectual assent than with habituation.

## What This Shifts

The wager is cited as a curiosity, sometimes as a weakness. It is in fact one of the first texts to treat a question of meaning as a problem of decision under uncertainty, and to accept that reason, at times, supplies not the answer but only the form of the choice.

carte.punch: Pascal's wager is not an argument for believing in God.
carte.idee: Pascal begins by admitting that reason cannot decide: “God is, or he is not... reason can determine nothing here.” The wager addresses the person whom proofs have not convinced, and it holds that one cannot abstain from betting.

quiz.question: On what premise does Pascal rest his whole wager?
choix: That the rational proofs of God's existence are ultimately convincing
That reason cannot decide, and yet one cannot abstain from wagering
That religious belief provides a happier life here and now
That doubt is a moral fault as much as an error of judgment
quiz.explication: Pascal grants from the outset that reason is powerless to establish God's existence; this is the starting point, not a late concession. The wager therefore addresses only the person whom proofs leave undecided, and it rests on the idea that one stakes one's life anyway: abstention is not an available option.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the oldest and strongest objection raised against Pascal's wager?
choix: The reasoning holds for any divinity promising an infinite gain, and these divinities exclude one another
The calculus of probabilities that Pascal was developing with Fermat does not apply to religious questions
No one can decide to believe in God by a mere calculation, even sincerely wanting to
A gain described as infinite has, according to the objectors, strictly no mathematical meaning
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The strongest objection, known as the competing gods objection, is that the reasoning works for any divinity promising an infinite gain, and that these divinities exclude one another.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Pascal answer the objection that one does not decide to believe as one decides to bet?
choix: He acknowledges that the objection is decisive and abandons his reasoning
He advises acting first, following the gestures and habits, admitting that conviction may follow
He asserts that sincere belief is not necessary to win the wager
He proposes replacing inner belief entirely with a mere public declaration of faith
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pascal advises acting first, following the gestures and habits, admitting that conviction may follow: belief, for him, has less to do with assent than with habituation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which tool had Pascal just developed, with Fermat, at the time of writing his wager?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pascal, who had just founded the calculus of probabilities in his correspondence with Fermat, applies his own tool here to an unexpected object, a wager on the existence of God.
